content: An alloy is a solid solution or a homogeneous mixture composed of two or more elements, with at least one being a metal. This mixture exhibits metallic properties. The properties of an alloy are often distinct from those of its individual components. By combining one metal with others, the resulting alloy frequently demonstrates enhanced characteristics. For example, steel, which is primarily composed of iron, is significantly stronger than pure iron. The physical properties of an alloy, such as density, reactivity, Young's modulus, and electrical or thermal conductivity, may not differ substantially from those of its constituent elements. However, its engineering properties, such as tensile strength and shear strength, can vary significantly. These differences often arise due to the atomic sizes of the elements within the alloy. Larger atoms exert compressive forces on neighboring atoms, while smaller atoms exert tensile forces, which collectively contribute to the alloy's resistance to deformation. Even minor variations in the composition of an alloy can lead to pronounced differences in its behavior. For instance, impurities in semiconducting ferromagnetic alloys can alter their properties, a phenomenon first predicted by White, Hogan, Suhl, Tian Abrie, and Nakamura. Some alloys are created by melting and mixing two or more metals. Brass, for example, is an alloy of copper and zinc, while bronze, commonly used for statues, ornaments, and church bells, is an alloy of tin and copper. Unlike pure metals, most alloys do not have a single melting point. Instead, they exhibit a melting range, during which the material exists as a mixture of solid and liquid phases. The temperature at which melting begins is referred to as the solidus, while the temperature at which melting is complete is called the liquidus. However, certain alloys have specific proportions of constituents that result in a single melting point or, in rare cases, two melting points. This is known as the alloy's eutectic mixture. Alloys can be classified based on the number of their constituent elements. A binary alloy contains two components, a ternary alloy contains three, and so on. Additionally, alloys can be categorized as substitution alloys or interstitial alloys, depending on their formation mechanism. In substitution alloys, the atoms of the components are of similar size, and the atoms simply replace one another within the crystal structure. Brass, a binary substitution alloy of copper and zinc, is an example. Interstitial alloys, on the other hand, form when the atoms of one component are significantly smaller than those of the other, allowing the smaller atoms to fit into the spaces (interstices) between the larger atoms. In practice, some alloys are so predominantly associated with their base metals that the name of the primary constituent is often used to refer to the alloy itself. For instance, 14-karat gold is an alloy of gold combined with other elements. Similarly, the silver used in jewelry and the aluminum used as a structural building material are also alloys. In everyday language, the term alloy is sometimes used as a shorthand for a specific alloy. For example, automobile wheels made of aluminum alloy are commonly referred to as alloy wheels. This usage is somewhat imprecise, as steels and most other metals in practical applications are also alloys.
